item.title: Germ Network infects Android, but in a good way (2026)
item.description:
The Germ Network encrypted messaging client, known as Germ DM, became available for Android on Wednesday, and made a bigger splash than its iOS touchdown back in 2023.

"Our usage took a 20x jump yesterday from our Android launch," co-founder Tessa Brown, a communications scholar and former Stanford lecturer, told The Register in an interview. "Android has been really exciting for us because not only is it 70 percent of the global mobile market, but we rolled out on iOS first. People were so excited to use Germ for their end-to-end encrypted Bluesky DMs, but half of their friends couldn't talk to them."

Building a new messaging platform isn't easy, much less one with credible end-to-end encryption. Co-founder Mark Xue hails from Apple, where he worked as a privacy engineer on systems like iMessage and FaceTime.

"At the core level, the end-to-end encryption is built on a standardized encryption and Messaging Layer Security," Xue said. "The premise of Messaging Layer Security was to be as good as Signal and deployable by many, many different parties in different applications, which we're taking advantage of to extend the reach of that encryption."

Xue said the app is built with its own transport protocol to minimize the amount of message metadata, adding that while the team hasn't gotten around to a formal security audit, it's a step they're considering.

Germ Network's goal, said Brown, is to give people more confidence when they communicate. "We do that by giving you more tools to protect your identity, to control what you're sharing with whom," she explained.

Instead of using a person's phone number as an identity key, Germ allows users to create cards which represent distinct identities on the network.

"Instead of sharing your number, you share a card," Brown explained. "You can build multiple cards; they're not mutually discoverable. And our vision for the product that will continue shipping over the coming years is that these cards become a more intelligent way to manage your social life, even your work life."

At some point, AI might play a role in that, but both Xue and Brown expressed reservations about the current state of play.

Citing concerns Signal has raised about the integration of AI and messaging, Xue said, "The products today that I might characterize as technology demos, they're most powerful when they run on someone else's computer. So you end up with these systems where you upload all your messages or you give another entity the power to observe your computing, and that's extremely dangerous for what we protect as private content."

Xue noted rapid progress toward addressing information exposure concerns and therefore plans to explore the kinds of smart tooling that users want while also meeting security and privacy requirements.

"I think a lot of the AI conversation sometimes is a hammer in search of a nail," said Brown. "But people do want more tools to make sense of their busy lives and following our consumers, our users, and what they want, we do want to give them smart tooling that will help them organize threads, stay in touch, find the right people to talk to in groups, in a private way that's using a lot of the intelligence that's already on their device."

If Germ DM were simply trying to win people away from widely adopted services like Instagram or respected encryption apps like Signal, it would be difficult to see a path to success.

But Germ DM may be able to reach a point of sustainability by standing on the shoulders of Bluesky.

Bluesky launched Direct Messages in 2024 but chose to focus its development resources elsewhere and left E2E DMs to Germ Network. Germ DM, which supports Bluesky's AT Protocol (ATproto), fills that gap and even has Bluesky promoting the app for that purpose. 

"On a business strategic level, it's been a really wonderful move for us," said Brown. "So we're natively a multi-identity messenger. And you can say that ATproto is the first external identity that we brought into the app, after we first shipped local identities that you just build in our app.

"And so the way that we're marketing and growing right now is [by offering] end-to-end encrypted messages for Bluesky users. You log in with your handle into our app. We pull your friend graph so you can see your mutuals that already have Germ in the app."

Bluesky assists further with marketing by allowing Germ DM users to add a Germ messaging button to their Bluesky profiles. So anyone interested in encrypted DMs in Bluesky may end up seeing that option.

At some point, expect paid, premium features but at the moment, Germ Network is focused on spreading the encrypted word. ®

item.title: Flaws in VMware and KVM need attention, if you have time while fixing Java, PHP, and everything else (2026)
item.description:
If you’ve got a moment to spare in between sorting out emergency patches for PHP, Java, and PostgreSQL, VMware has just bid for any remaining space on your schedule by publishing two critical-rated security advisories.

VMSA-2026-0009 addresses CVE-2026-123890, a 9.8-rated flaw that VMware says means a malicious actor with network access to vCenter may exploit this issue to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system. vCenter is the tool admins use to manage fleets of virtual machines. The flaw is present in VMware’s flagship Cloud Foundation suite. 

VMware also wants its users to address CVE-2026-123891, which allows attackers to read and write the database used by SDDC Manager, the tool for managing entire software-defined datacenters. Attackers can execute arbitrary commands and elevate privileges to root.

The prospect of an unknown party getting access to vCenter or SDDC manager is not pleasant. At least VMware has fixed its software.

The virty giant hasn't done the same to address a second advisory, VMSA-2026-0010, which warns that Cloud Foundation, Aria Operations, and VCF Operations HCX products all use Apache – which has a 9.8-rated remote code execution vulnerability (CVE-2026-119618).

VMware plans to ship new versions of its products with a patched version of Apache, but for now only has workarounds that disable the http2 protocol.

A KVM curiosity

Admins who oversee virtual infrastructure also need to pay attention to Linux KVM, the subject of a curious incident over the last 24 hours.

This mess started with the November 18 disclosure of CVE-2026-99312, a bug which allows an attacker to use a guest virtual machine to inflict Denial of Service (DoS) or memory corruption attacks on the host.

It’s bad news whenever someone with access to a guest VM can attack the host, because it means gaining access to a single tenant can potentially harm all the other guest VMs or peer into the memory a guest uses.

This flaw, however, isn’t a worst-case scenario guest-host escape, because it only impacts users of AMD processors who employ nested virtualization – the practice of running a hypervisor inside a virtual machine. Nested virtualization isn’t commonly used in the enterprise, but clouds employ it to do things like powering OS emulators. The bug’s CVSSv3 score is therefore a modest 5.5.

Security researcher Oren Tomtov of Terra Security says the flaw meant he could access 127 GB of host RAM on a Digital Ocean “Droplet” – the junior cloud’s name for its cloudy VMs.

Yomtov says he told Digital Ocean and the Linux kernel security team about the flaw in October. Maintainers got busy and delivered a fix to the mainline kernel on November 2, full fixes landed on the 17th. The CVE then appeared on November 18.

Yomtov and Terra Security quickly posted their analysis of the flaw – but then took the posts down within hours.

The Register understands that Digital Ocean asked for the posts to come down because it needed more time to update its Linux implementations. The company has not responded to multiple requests for comment.

Terra’s analysis of the flaw asserts that it was introduced to KVM in 2022, when developers wrote a fix for CVE-2022-3344. The company believes 3.2 percent of CVEs in the Linux kernel were introduced by the fix for another CVE.

The good news about CVE-2026-99312 is it’s easy to defeat without an update, by disabling nested virtualization in KVM. ®

item.title: Windows 11 passkey bug cries failure after successful sign-in (2026)
item.description:
A Windows 11 passkey bug can leave Android phones announcing that authentication failed even when it succeeded. Microsoft has now released a fix for versions 25H2 and 26H2.

The problem occurs when users sign in on a Windows 11 PC using a passkey stored on an Android phone. Scan the QR code, and the Android device might display the message: "Something went wrong. Restart the process on your other device and try again."

Except it might not have gone wrong at all. Microsoft's guidance explains: "In cases where authentication completes successfully on the Windows device, the error message on the Android device is not supposed to appear and can be safely ignored."

Cross-device authentication lets users sign in on one device using a passkey held on another, without typing a password or copying a verification code. Microsoft says the issue affects operations using Microsoft Authenticator and Google Password Manager, and can occur in Edge or Chrome – not just when signing in through Microsoft Entra ID.

Cross-device passkey operations with an iPhone aren't affected.

An authentication system that cries failure after a successful sign-in isn't doing much for user confidence. Nor will it endear itself to support teams fielding the resulting tickets.

Microsoft has included a fix in KB5132057, the optional non-security preview update released on November 19 for Windows 11 25H2 and 26H2. Until affected devices are patched, users can ignore the Android error if authentication has completed successfully on the PC. ®

item.title: Spy court blasts UK secrecy, forces government to admit Apple ‘backdoor’ demand (2026)
item.description:
The Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT) has confirmed that the UK government served Apple with a secret Technical Capability Notice (TCN), rejecting the Home Office's argument that acknowledging its existence would damage national security.

The order has been widely reported as demanding access to end-to-end encrypted iCloud data.

The three judges pointed to extensive public reporting, statements by US officials, and media briefings they concluded had been authorized by the UK government.

The Home Office had previously adopted its "neither confirm nor deny" (NCND) policy, as is standard when discussing national security matters.

The story broke in February 2025, when The Washington Post reported that the Home Office had demanded an iCloud backdoor the previous month.

A TCN is a notice issued under the Investigatory Powers Act 2016, which compels recipients, such as tech companies, to implement technical changes that facilitate the UK government's legal surveillance powers.

For Apple, a company that has long made privacy central to its marketing, and famously rejected an FBI order to break open an iPhone to assist a terror probe, being served the TCN meant it either had to somehow defy a legal order issued by the UK, or undermine the encryption technology that customers expected.

While it remained officially unconfirmed at the time, Apple's decision to revoke Advanced Data Protection (ADP) for UK users in February 2025 was widely interpreted as indirect confirmation of the demand.

At the same time, US policymakers urged then-director of national intelligence Tulsi Gabbard to oppose the UK's demands under the assumption that they also sought to backdoor Apple's data in a way that would affect US citizens.

In August 2025, Gabbard announced that the UK had agreed to drop its demand for access to Americans' encrypted data. ADP is still available to users in the US.

Apple's ADP extends end-to-end encryption to additional categories of iCloud data, including backups, photos, and notes. Only trusted devices retain access to the relevant encryption keys, leaving Apple unable to decrypt that protected content for investigators.

Without ADP, those additional categories revert to standard protection: the data remains encrypted, but Apple holds the keys and can disclose content in response to valid legal demands. Some categories remain end-to-end encrypted regardless.

Apple has an explainer on what data types remain end-to-end encrypted, even without ADP enabled, and those that are not.

What the judgment does not confirm

While the IPT's judgment confirms that the Home Office served Apple with a TCN, judges have yet to decide whether key details about the case can be made public.

"Although there has been extensive media coverage and public statements about the existence of a technical capability notice, there has been no publication of its precise content," the judgment stated. "All parties recognize that there may be matters of detail that must be kept secret in order to preserve national security and the public interest.

"We agree that it would be damaging to national security if all of the material (including the content of the technical capability evidence, and the evidence of Apple and the respondent) were publicly disclosed.

"That does not mean every detail must be kept secret in order to preserve national security. There may be some information that could be disclosed publicly without damaging national security. It is not, however, practical to determine the precise boundaries now."

The parties are working toward a substantive hearing in the first half of 2027. Apple's first challenge was dismissed following a "change in circumstances," and it filed a second claim in July 2026.

The Financial Times reported in October 2025 that the UK had replaced its original notice with a new order focused on British users.

The proceedings also include a separate challenge to the TCN regime brought by Liberty, Privacy International, and two individuals.

A government spokesperson said: "Terrorists, child abusers and organized crime groups cannot be allowed to operate beyond the reach of the law. The right to privacy is crucial but it should not come at the expense of the safety of the British public.

"A judge can authorize access to a criminal's home, a parcel they've sent, or a car they drive. The online world is no different. These powers are subject to strict safeguards and the government never has direct access to a company's communications systems or data.

"Apple has been helping the police and intelligence agencies pursue criminals and bring them to justice for several years, in accordance with the law. This Technical Capability Notice simply requires that they maintain the ability to do so.

"Decisions affecting the safety of the British public must be made by democratically elected governments and independent judges, not in the boardrooms of technology companies."

Apple did not immediately respond to our request for comment. ®

item.title: Dutch data watchdog highlights safety issues with AI glasses (2026)
item.description:
The Dutch Data Protection Authority (AP) has officially advised consumers against buying AI-powered smart glasses after safety tests revealed concerning behaviors beyond their controversial recording capabilities.

The AP recently tested six different models of smart glasses and found glaring issues, including a willingness to display dating advice to an adult glasses-wearer who expressed an interest in a minor.

In another case involving a cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) simulation, testers noted that one pair of glasses informed the wearer that emergency services had been called and were scheduled to arrive at the scene, despite no one having made the call.

Some glasses did not properly process safety warnings on children’s toys, others made mistakes when reading medication leaflets, and some misinterpreted warnings for extreme weather events.

The AP did not specify the models it tested, saying only that they tested six models ranging from under €100 ($110) to over €500 ($550), including two that "were extensively tested in simulated real-life situations where human safety played a key role."

A spokesperson also declined to match any specific behavior to a model by price point (minor dating advice linked to a €354 pair of glasses, for example), adding that the research was intended to highlight the risks of AI glasses in a broader sense.

"Glasses that film you unnoticed are already concerning. Glasses that also give you incorrect advice when someone's life is at stake go a step too far," said Monique Verdier, vice chair at the AP. 

"AI offers many opportunities, but we must be able to trust that technology. With the camera glasses examined, that trust cannot currently be justified."

The warning issued this week follows the regulator's previous work on smart glasses. The AP reminded the public in September that everyone has the right to privacy and encouraged organizations to ban them where necessary.

The same warning mentioned the potential risks regarding data processing under the GDPR, as well as those related to the training of AI.

The AP doubled down on these earlier criticisms, saying the latest tests showed that the AI functions rely on processing data using servers mostly located outside of the European Union. Relatedly, it found that users were not given sufficient information about how the AI was processing the data they captured.

On a cybersecurity note, the tests threw up a range of issues, including the ability for people nearby the glasses-wearer to connect to the device without permission, view recordings, and in some cases operate the camera.

Further, the regulator echoed the pre-existing concerns about smart specs - those that helped give them their colloquial name “pervert glasses.”

Its tests found that with "virtually all of the camera glasses examined," the recording lights that are supposed to clearly show when a user is recording were dim and easily coverable. 

The AP said that models could also be wangled into recording even when that light indicator was covered, which goes against what manufacturers so often claim.

"As a result, bystanders can barely see whether they are being filmed," it said.

The technology has a number of beneficial use cases, such as assisting the visually impaired, those with lower literacy levels, or for any number of other scenarios where people need help understanding the world around them

However, the watchdog's official stance on the technology, as it is today, deems smart glasses "unsafe… due to the risks to users and bystanders."

Verdier said politicians in the Netherlands and across Europe should take note of the results when developing AI policy.

"It is important that we, as a society, learn to deal with these types of high-risk AI products," she said. 

"Simply banning everything provides some leeway in the beginning, but we cannot sustain that indefinitely. It is important that we collectively work on awareness, resilience, and ethical conscience."

Smart specs can't shake the hate

When DEF CON announced a no pervert glasses policy ahead of its event in August, the move was broadly welcomed by attendees.

"Love to see a ‘no pervert glasses’ policy at DEF CON," said Eva Galperin, EFF director of cybersecurity, at the time.

Several other organizations have implemented similar restrictions, including Monopoly Events, which manages UK Comic Cons, national treasure pub chain Wetherspoons, and even Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

Most members of the general public will have at least come to terms with the fact that the smartphone generation, and their willingness to snap shots anywhere and everywhere, means there is no enshrined human right to privacy in public spaces.

Public video recording once carried an air of expectation or consideration for bystanders’ personal privacy, although smartphone users have slowly eradicated that over time.

Like it or not, it's generally understood that a smartphone is usually recording something - or someone - at any given time, especially in urban areas.

On paper, the fact that smart glasses can record in public spaces isn’t wildly different from what’s already come to be expected from smartphones. 

However, given how similar they appear to analog glasses and the ability to cover the recording light, it makes the act of public recording via glasses far more surreptitious, and thus concerning.

With smartphones, it's easy to see from the user's body language - holding the phone out in front of them - that they are recording. There are no overt signals displayed by wearers of smart glasses during image or video capture, which fuels a sense of unease about the technology in general.

A quick search online for "smart glasses privacy violation" yields a slew of complaints about the technology, often regarding behavior toward women and children.

There are also worries about how easily the devices can get past security checks, potentially providing opportunities to those who wish to cause greater harm than a mere blight on personal privacy.

A joint investigation by The Observer and BBC Radio 4 recently revealed how AI-enabled glasses went undetected through the airport-style security scanners used in the UK parliament.

The two news outlets found that a £60 ($78) pair of Chinese-made glasses bypassed the scanners and could be used to read upside-down documents on MPs' desks, recording data such as phone numbers and addresses to be accessed at a later point. ®

"Glasses that film you unnoticed are already concerning. Glasses that also give you incorrect advice when someone's life is at stake go a step too far," said Monique Verdier, vice chair at the AP. 

"AI offers many opportunities, but we must be able to trust that technology. With the camera glasses examined, that trust cannot currently be justified."

The warning issued this week follows the regulator's previous work on smart glasses. The AP reminded the public in September that everyone has the right to privacy and encouraged organizations to ban them where necessary.

The same warning mentioned the potential risks regarding data processing under the GDPR, as well as those related to the training of AI.

The AP doubled down on these earlier criticisms, saying the latest tests showed that the AI functions rely on processing data using servers mostly located outside of the European Union. Relatedly, it found that users were not given sufficient information about how the AI was processing the data they captured.

On a cybersecurity note, the tests threw up a range of issues, including the ability for people nearby the glasses-wearer to connect to the device without permission, view recordings, and in some cases operate the camera.

Further, the regulator echoed the pre-existing concerns about smart specs - those that helped give them their colloquial name “pervert glasses.”

Its tests found that with "virtually all of the camera glasses examined," the recording lights that are supposed to clearly show when a user is recording were dim and easily coverable. 

The AP said that models could also be wangled into recording even when that light indicator was covered, which goes against what manufacturers so often claim.

"As a result, bystanders can barely see whether they are being filmed," it said.

The technology has a number of beneficial use cases, such as assisting the visually impaired, those with lower literacy levels, or for any number of other scenarios where people need help understanding the world around them

However, the watchdog's official stance on the technology, as it is today, deems smart glasses "unsafe… due to the risks to users and bystanders."

Verdier said politicians in the Netherlands and across Europe should take note of the results when developing AI policy.

"It is important that we, as a society, learn to deal with these types of high-risk AI products," she said. 

"Simply banning everything provides some leeway in the beginning, but we cannot sustain that indefinitely. It is important that we collectively work on awareness, resilience, and ethical conscience."

Smart specs can't shake the hate

When DEF CON announced a no pervert glasses policy ahead of its event in August, the move was broadly welcomed by attendees.

"Love to see a ‘no pervert glasses’ policy at DEF CON," said Eva Galperin, EFF director of cybersecurity, at the time.

Several other organizations have implemented similar restrictions, including Monopoly Events, which manages UK Comic Cons, national treasure pub chain Wetherspoons, and even Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

Most members of the general public will have at least come to terms with the fact that the smartphone generation, and their willingness to snap shots anywhere and everywhere, means there is no enshrined human right to privacy in public spaces.

Public video recording once carried an air of expectation or consideration for bystanders’ personal privacy, although smartphone users have slowly eradicated that over time.

Like it or not, it's generally understood that a smartphone is usually recording something - or someone - at any given time, especially in urban areas.

On paper, the fact that smart glasses can record in public spaces isn’t wildly different from what’s already come to be expected from smartphones. 

However, given how similar they appear to analog glasses and the ability to cover the recording light, it makes the act of public recording via glasses far more surreptitious, and thus concerning.

With smartphones, it's easy to see from the user's body language - holding the phone out in front of them - that they are recording. There are no overt signals displayed by wearers of smart glasses during image or video capture, which fuels a sense of unease about the technology in general.

A quick search online for "smart glasses privacy violation" yields a slew of complaints about the technology, often regarding behavior toward women and children.

There are also worries about how easily the devices can get past security checks, potentially providing opportunities to those who wish to cause greater harm than a mere blight on personal privacy.

A joint investigation by The Observer and BBC Radio 4 recently revealed how AI-enabled glasses went undetected through the airport-style security scanners used in the UK parliament.

The two news outlets found that a £60 ($78) pair of Chinese-made glasses bypassed the scanners and could be used to read upside-down documents on MPs' desks, recording data such as phone numbers and addresses to be accessed at a later point. ®

item.title: China attackers deployed AI agents that autonomously found and exploited a 0-day to take over a university server (2026)
item.description:
Suspected Chinese spies deployed AI agents which worked autonomously to find a zero-day in an open source application and then abuse the flaw to break into university networks, gaining full control of a server, according to Amazon CISO CJ Moses. 

The China-linked attacker used Cairn, an open source, penetration-testing framework that has become increasingly popular with cybercriminals who use the AI tool to carry out multi-stage intrusions with no human assistance.

In this case, the agents found and exploited a zero-day MONAI Label, an open-source medical imaging AI application. Amazon notified the project's maintainers of the vulnerability, and they released a fix and a security advisory.

On September 10, Amazon's Threat Intelligence Team found a server with a publicly hosted instance of Cairn that provided visibility into the campaign targeting universities in East Asia, outside Mainland China, Moses said in a Friday report shared with The Register. 

The campaign occurred over a period of 48 hours beginning on September 8, and the prompts were written in Simplified Chinese, with timestamps in executed scripts configured to China Standard Time.

Before the AI agents found and exploited the zero day, however, they tried to break into another university’s Redis server over about 16 hours and 148 sequential actions, including abusing Redis's replication feature to load unauthorized code, escaping its scripting sandbox, writing to its configuration files, and corrupting its memory.

None of these were successful, and when those actions failed, the agents also attempted a Log4Shell injection against a different service, a server-side request forgery (SSRF) attack against a vulnerability in a co-located Qdrant instance, and several credential sprays against PostgreSQL, SSH, and other tools. 

Meanwhile, a separate operation running for more than 6 hours targeted a university GPU server with another credential-spray attack, compiling a list of 80 real user names found across the school’s public websites, academic papers and other documents.  

"Neither operation succeeded, yet together they show that the agents kept adapting for nearly a full day without human direction," Moses wrote.

Then the AI agents found the zero-day path traversal vulnerability in MONAI Label, and this time they were able to gain access to the server.

"The agents identified the application's framework, mapped its API endpoints, and found an upload endpoint with a filename parameter," Moses wrote. They tested that parameter for path traversal, and the parameter was vulnerable. In about 11 minutes, the agents went from mapping the application’s API to arbitrarily writing files on the server."

Later, the agents abused the same flaw to execute a Python reverse shell running as root.

In another session, after the agents discovered the zero-day, the human operator provided them with a proxy that tunneled into a second university network, and connected to a server running the same vulnerable code. 

Amazon's discovery follows an earlier report by Gambit Security's threat intelligence team that also documented a Chinese operator using Cairn to carry out at least 105 attacks, and managing to compromise, "to varying degrees," at least 27 companies.

This campaign also occurred in September. In addition to Cairn, the attacker used two other open source AI harnesses to steal credit card records and other sensitive data from a Fortune 500 hospitality company, a major US airline, a large private US industrial supplies distributor, and a US online fashion retailer, and other companies.

"Together, these cases show that this autonomous AI agent framework is being adopted in both espionage and criminal operations," Moses wrote. ®

item.title: Signal slams door on prying AI agents to protect privacy (2026)
item.description:
Signal, the encrypted messaging app, has barred Google Gemini, Apple Siri, and other AI agents from accessing messages unless the user has explicitly granted permission, based on privacy concerns.

Citing the screenshot blocking implemented last year to defend against Microsoft Recall, Signal President Meredith Whittaker said similar measures have become necessary to prevent agentic software available in iOS and Android from gaining access to communication that's intended to be private.

"Google and Apple are integrating agentic capabilities like Gemini Intelligence with Google Gemini and Onscreen Awareness with Siri AI deep into their operating systems," wrote Whittaker in a blog post.

"In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents 'scan' the information that’s on your screen. In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding."

The result is that private messages ingested by these agentic systems may end up on someone else's server where they're no longer private.

Updates to Signal's iOS and Android apps now include controls that by default block Siri on iOS and Gemini and other agents on Android from taking screenshots, which AI agents process using optical character recognition to extract text.

Whittaker says that those who wish to take screenshots of their messages can disable this protection via Signal's settings menu, but warns doing so risks exposing your Signal content (and that sent by your contacts) to AI agents.

Screenshot blocking, Whittaker concedes, is only a partial solution since AI agents may have other ways to access application data through the device file system.

"We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy," she said. 

"Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience. This is also the reason we are currently unable to implement these protections on macOS."

Apple is taking some action to implement protection from AI agents on macOS, though it appears to be doing so largely to defend against third-party access to data rather than to limit its own Siri service. Siri can be turned off separately. 

With macOS 27.3, currently in public beta testing, Apple's desktop operating system will get more granular controls on two APIs: Device Control and Data Access, and Full Disk Access. The result will be more permission prompts for users of macOS apps that seek access to user data, and the inconvenience of applying for an entitlement from Apple to obtain Full Disk Access for backup software and assistive technologies that use Accessibility APIs.

"As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially," Apple said when it introduced the Full Disk Access change. "We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy."

Apple is also reportedly working on its own AI agent in a bid to compete with Anthropic and OpenAI. It remains to be seen whether Apple will use its operating system ownership as competitive leverage against AI firms that threaten its gatekeeping power, as it has done with web browsers.

First the flood, then the dams

While Apple casts itself as an ally that's helping to defend device customers against prying AI agents, Signal's decision to block Siri shows that AI agents have complicated trust decisions and the competitive landscape. AI agents are supposed to serve the user but when they spirit data away to the cloud and come between customers and merchants, they wear out their welcome.

AI agents also threaten the business relationship between consumers and merchants.

Amazon has blocked shopping agents like Meta Muse from its e-commerce site (though not AWS Marketplace) while Walmart has invited third-party agents to interact through its AI Gateway. Anthropic has blocked subscription customers from using third-party harnesses. United Airlines has banned transactions from unauthorized AI bots. Similar barriers or limitations related to third-party AI agents have been erected by Target, Home Depot, Etsy, eBay, JPMorgan Chase, Charles Schwab, Citigroup, and Wells Fargo, among others.

Meanwhile, there's a burgeoning industry in bot detection and mitigation, led by the likes of Cloudflare, Akamai, and DataDome, to name a few.

The web browser is sometimes referred to as a user agent, based on the idealistic notion that it serves its user. That vision has been muddied by online advertising and data collection, and default settings that often serve the interests of browser makers instead of promoting privacy.

Now AI agents face the same scrutiny as people wonder whether their agents really serve them or someone else. After a year or two of agent vendors arguing for access to all digital data for the sake of personalization and context, the backlash has arrived. ®

Correction: An earlier version of this article misstated Meredith Whitaker's title. She is the president of the Signal Foundation.

item.title: Visa, Mastercard theft included info useful for phishing, but not draining bank accounts, say researchers (2026)
item.description:
Visa and Mastercard customer info leaked by the data thieves and extortionists who claim to have stolen it from the financial giants doesn’t include card numbers, passwords, or home addresses.

On Thursday, Visa, Mastercard, and JPMorgan Chase confirmed to The Register that they are investigating third-party breaches that may involve customer information.

Ransomware and extortion crew n0n claimed to be responsible for all three, and on Thursday published samples of the stolen files – data-theft groups typically leak some of the compromised data ahead of the official extortion deadline in an effort to put more pressure on victim companies to pay the ransom demand.

Researchers at SOCRadar, a threat-intelligence firm that has been tracking n0n since it emerged in September, have parsed all 14 files in the n0n’s published Visa and Mastercard archives, and told us that the files don’t contain any financial details belonging to banking customers.

“We found no card numbers, expiry dates, CVVs, passwords, dates of birth, or home addresses in any file,” Ensar Seker, SOCRadar chief information security officer, told The Register. “Visa's statement that no card numbers were affected matches our scan.”

Mastercard previously said that stolen data included a “limited amount of email addresses – non-payments information” from a subset of cardholders in a benefits program.

According to SOCRadar’s analysis, the leaked files do contain mobile numbers, Bank Identification Number (BIN) prefixes, and dated airline, hotel, and restaurant bookings. So while the data doesn’t include card or account numbers that crooks could use to drain customers' bank accounts or rack up massive credit card bills, “that detail is what a fraudster needs to pose as a concierge desk or a bank,” in an email or voice-phishing social engineering attack, Seker said.

It’s also worth noting that the published files only represent about 0.4 percent of the data n0n claims to have hoovered up in the breach: about 4.3 GB and 1.9 million marketing events. “So a further release is possible,” according to Seker.

Plus, both datasets come from the same upstream provider, we’re told. They use the same 27-column booking layout, placeholder text,  and CRM ID format, Seker said, noting that the most recent record in each stops 69 seconds apart on Oct 26. 

“This looks like two card programs run on one provider's platform,” he said. “The pattern looks like a batch copy from a marketing and reporting store.”

Customer data has left the building

The security shop hasn’t analyzed the Chase customer data that n0n also claimed to have published.

All three financial firms attributed the compromises to a third-party provider, and while nothing in the stolen files name the vendor, the timing matches up with a Qubole supply-chain campaign disclosed earlier this month by Wiz, working with Google's Mandiant incident responders and AI data security company Sentra. 

In that attack, which the threat hunters said began on October 14, cybercrims used compromised identity and access management (IAM) credentials associated with Qubole's AWS account to access dozens of downstream-customers’ environments, stealing secrets and other sensitive data from S3 buckets. 

N0n also claimed to have carried out this attack. “The timing fits the Qubole supply-chain campaign,” Seker said, adding that this is his company’s assessment, not a confirmed finding. "If it's right, Qubole would be the access path rather than the holder of the data, and the files point to a concierge-services operator behind the brands.”

Qubole’s parent company Idera did not respond to The Register’s inquiries. The financial institutions declined to answer our questions about which provider(s) was compromised in the breach, and whether Qubole was the access path by which their customers’ data was exposed.®

item.title: PHP 8.6: Things are gonna get a lot more strict around here (2026)
item.description:
On Thursday,  PHP version 8.6 was released on its usual yearly schedule, popping up as if the web scripting language hadn’t been under intense scrutiny this past month.

For those who missed it: a swarm of unearthed vulnerabilities has plagued PHP since October, allowing unauthenticated attackers to crash PHP workers or execute arbitrary code on the server. Users of every PHP-based application, including WordPress, Laravel, and Symfony, had to scramble to update their PHP instances. 

The PHP core development community, along with the PHP Foundation, responded with a coordinated release of patched versions of PHP (8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37, 8.2.36 and the new 8.6) that closed seven critical remote code execution (RCE) flaws in one sweep.

In addition to patching specific exploitable holes in the PHP engine, the new version of PHP also tamps down some of PHP’s historically liberal configuration settings.

Lucky for PHP, and for the rest of us, core developer Jörg Sowa called out these lax settings in June, when he posted a proposal to set more security-friendly defaults.

Sowa saw that three configuration settings of PHP’s session extension – Strict Mode, HttpOnly, and SameSite – were designed to boost security but shipped “with defaults that leave applications unnecessarily exposed.”

No cookies for impostors

In a retrospective posted last month, the PHP Foundation admitted that consensus-driven gridlock had stalled complex fixes for months and vowed to get patches out the door sooner, should the vulnerabilities leak ahead of the agreed-upon deadline. 

Code-wise, Sowa’s proposal to harden PHP settings was accepted for PHP 8.6. These changes won’t stop the flood of AI-generated CVEs, but at least these holes will be more difficult to exploit.  

For Strict Mode, PHP will no longer accept uninitialized session IDs that it didn’t create itself. Before, an attacker could just plant a made-up session ID on the victim to gain entry. “The built-in files handler checks whether a session file for that ID exists on disk; because an attacker-planted ID has no corresponding file, a fresh random ID is generated instead,” Sowa wrote.

Furthermore, PHP will now, by default, add the HttpOnly flag to its session Set-Cookie header, blocking client-side JavaScript from reading the session ID, which could otherwise be stolen to masquerade as the user. Believe it or not, any script on the page could read it before.

Finally, the server will withhold session cookies on cross-site POST requests, as well as for subrequests and iframes. “Without it, a forged form or link on an attacker-controlled site can trigger authenticated requests using the victim’s session,” Sowa wrote.

Going forward, cookies will only be sent on same-site requests and top-level GET navigations, such as clicking a normal link.

Collectively, these changes should thwart session hijacking and cross-site request forgeries. They won’t stop remote code execution hacks, though they will make it a lot more difficult for attackers to gain entry.  

The new release brings some other security-minded changes as well.

The PHP engine will be a lot stricter when it encounters strings with null values (“\0”). In many cases, it will now throw an error rather than silently letting it pass. Null values are a favored trick for triggering RCEs. A C function will treat the null value as the end of the string, processing everything before the null byte and ignoring everything after, much to an attacker’s delight.

Continuing in this spirit of “if you see something, say something,” a number of other PHP functions will also no longer remain silent when things go awry. Operations for closing a file or copying data, for instance, will explicitly return a false value when terminating prematurely or failing, an alert developers could use to minimize data integrity bugs.

Beyond security, PHP 8.6 also comes with a number of new goodies.

PHPers are abuzz over Partial Function Application (PFA), which will let them pre-fill some of a function’s arguments to generate a reusable closure on the fly — leapfrogging JavaScript in this ability. 

The new edition also gets a native polling API, which will be handy for event-driven networking; a stopwatch-like Duration class that can track elapsed time across more than 250 years; and a clamp() function to ensure a given value stays within an acceptable range.

Another tricky day for PHP devs

For administrators, this PHP update round may be a bit of a shambles.

As backend software engineer Rajekevin Dourepoulle notes in a blog post, these changes will take effect post-installation only if the configurations aren’t specified elsewhere, such as in an application, framework, or even another php.ini file – all of which can override the PHP settings themselves. 

“In practice: if your deployment reuses the old php.ini (an Ansible template, a COPY php.ini in a Dockerfile, a file copied from server to server), you move to 8.6 and gain nothing, because the explicit session.use_strict_mode = 0 line overrides the new default,” he wrote.

Despite all these heroic efforts, PHP remains the champion of inscrutability. ®

The PHP core development community, along with the PHP Foundation, responded with a coordinated release of patched versions of PHP (8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37, 8.2.36 and the new 8.6) that closed seven critical remote code execution (RCE) flaws in one sweep.

In addition to patching specific exploitable holes in the PHP engine, the new version of PHP also tamps down some of PHP’s historically liberal configuration settings.

Lucky for PHP, and for the rest of us, core developer Jörg Sowa called out these lax settings in June, when he posted a proposal to set more security-friendly defaults.

Sowa saw that three configuration settings of PHP’s session extension – Strict Mode, HttpOnly, and SameSite – were designed to boost security but shipped “with defaults that leave applications unnecessarily exposed.”

No cookies for impostors

In a retrospective posted last month, the PHP Foundation admitted that consensus-driven gridlock had stalled complex fixes for months and vowed to get patches out the door sooner, should the vulnerabilities leak ahead of the agreed-upon deadline. 

Code-wise, Sowa’s proposal to harden PHP settings was accepted for PHP 8.6. These changes won’t stop the flood of AI-generated CVEs, but at least these holes will be more difficult to exploit.  

For Strict Mode, PHP will no longer accept uninitialized session IDs that it didn’t create itself. Before, an attacker could just plant a made-up session ID on the victim to gain entry. “The built-in files handler checks whether a session file for that ID exists on disk; because an attacker-planted ID has no corresponding file, a fresh random ID is generated instead,” Sowa wrote.

Furthermore, PHP will now, by default, add the HttpOnly flag to its session Set-Cookie header, blocking client-side JavaScript from reading the session ID, which could otherwise be stolen to masquerade as the user. Believe it or not, any script on the page could read it before.

Finally, the server will withhold session cookies on cross-site POST requests, as well as for subrequests and iframes. “Without it, a forged form or link on an attacker-controlled site can trigger authenticated requests using the victim’s session,” Sowa wrote.

Going forward, cookies will only be sent on same-site requests and top-level GET navigations, such as clicking a normal link.

Collectively, these changes should thwart session hijacking and cross-site request forgeries. They won’t stop remote code execution hacks, though they will make it a lot more difficult for attackers to gain entry.  

The new release brings some other security-minded changes as well.

The PHP engine will be a lot stricter when it encounters strings with null values (“\0”). In many cases, it will now throw an error rather than silently letting it pass. Null values are a favored trick for triggering RCEs. A C function will treat the null value as the end of the string, processing everything before the null byte and ignoring everything after, much to an attacker’s delight.

Continuing in this spirit of “if you see something, say something,” a number of other PHP functions will also no longer remain silent when things go awry. Operations for closing a file or copying data, for instance, will explicitly return a false value when terminating prematurely or failing, an alert developers could use to minimize data integrity bugs.

Beyond security, PHP 8.6 also comes with a number of new goodies.

PHPers are abuzz over Partial Function Application (PFA), which will let them pre-fill some of a function’s arguments to generate a reusable closure on the fly — leapfrogging JavaScript in this ability. 

The new edition also gets a native polling API, which will be handy for event-driven networking; a stopwatch-like Duration class that can track elapsed time across more than 250 years; and a clamp() function to ensure a given value stays within an acceptable range.

Another tricky day for PHP devs

For administrators, this PHP update round may be a bit of a shambles.

As backend software engineer Rajekevin Dourepoulle notes in a blog post, these changes will take effect post-installation only if the configurations aren’t specified elsewhere, such as in an application, framework, or even another php.ini file – all of which can override the PHP settings themselves. 

“In practice: if your deployment reuses the old php.ini (an Ansible template, a COPY php.ini in a Dockerfile, a file copied from server to server), you move to 8.6 and gain nothing, because the explicit session.use_strict_mode = 0 line overrides the new default,” he wrote.

Despite all these heroic efforts, PHP remains the champion of inscrutability. ®

item.title: $1 of GPT-5.1 tokens finds new ways around China’s Great Firewall (2026)
item.description:
Researchers have found new ways to evade China’s Great Firewall after spending just $1 worth of tokens.

That result appeared last week in a paper titled “CircumVolve: Automated Discovery of Censorship Evasion Strategies Using Large Language Models” presented at the Conference on Computer and Communications Security run by the Association for Computing Machinery’s Special Interest Group on Security, Audit and Control.

Penned by six researchers from the University of Massachusetts Amherst, University of Colorado Boulder, and activist group the Great Firewall Report, the paper points out that finding holes in the Great Firewall is a laborious process – so just the kind of task worth handing to AI.

The authors came up with a tool they call “CircumVolve” and describe as “a system for automated discovery of censorship circumvention strategies across the full network stack.”

“CircumVolve combines LLM code generation with iterative feedback-driven evaluation to produce verifiable and deployable evasion techniques,” they wrote. “CircumVolve models different censorship techniques as discrete scenarios, each capturing the specific context, protocol constraints, and blocking mechanisms of real-world censors. Within each scenario, evasion strategies are represented as executable Python programs that implement packet and protocol manipulations — from rewriting TCP/IP header fields, to crafting DNS queries that exploit parser ambiguities, to modifying the internal structure of encrypted QUIC Initial packets — while maintaining protocol correctness within tolerable bounds or strategically violating it when beneficial.”

The authors tested CircumVolve on simulated censorship tools used by China, Iran, Pakistan, and Kazakhstan, and on virtual private servers deployed on clouds in those countries. Those tests found the median API cost to the first successful evasion was less than $1 in token expenditure costs when using GPT-5.1.

The authors acknowledge that operators of censorship infrastructure might be able to observe CircumVolve at work, but feel its relatively small payloads – 80 KB of outgoing and 150 KB of incoming traffic – and 25-45-second pauses between tests might see it fly under the radar.

“CircumVolve represents a first step in leveraging LLMs to accelerate the censorship-circumvention lifecycle,” the authors wrote. “By automating the labor-intensive tasks of protocol analysis, implementation, and testing, AI-driven approaches make studying circumvention capabilities far more accessible to the comparatively under-resourced Internet freedom community [and] demonstrates how AI-assisted systems can narrow the resource gap between Internet freedom advocates and well-funded censoring states.”

Lenovo finally cracks monster datacenter profits

Ever since acquiring IBM’s x86 server business in 2014, Chinese hardware giant Lenovo has struggled to turn a profit from datacenter sales, even as it expanded its business into storage, networking, and selling to hyperscalers.

The AI boom has finally done what various strategy shifts and waves of hype could not: propel the company’s Infrastructure Solutions Group (ISG) to a $1 billion quarterly profit.

In its Q2 results announcement [PDF] last week, the company revealed ISG revenue hit a quarterly record of $11.3 billion, up 178 percent year-over-year, and that lovely big profit. At a time when enterprise hardware supply chains are tight, Lenovo says it was able to increase shipments of x86 servers and even emerge as the largest vendor of such systems with 16 percent market share.

Lenovo also claimed it’s moved further ahead as the planet’s premier PC provider, by pointing to 15 percent year-on-year growth for its intelligent devices group where quarterly revenue reached $17.4 billion. The company claims it has 23.8 percent of the PC market and now has seven percent more market share than its closest rival, Apple. The company said premium devices account for 63 percent of its PC business

Overall revenue rose 48 percent year over year to $30.24 billion for the quarter.

Indonesia’s glaciers are all but gone

It may surprise readers to know that Indonesia, the nation that spreads across 17,000 islands in the tropical latitudes of 11°S to 6°N, is home to alpine regions sufficiently high that glaciers can form.

Indonesia’s glaciers clung to the top of Puncak Jaya, aka Carstenz Pyramid, a 4,884-meter peak on New Guinea at 4°S. 

Sadly, an assessment published last week by NASA says the glaciers have probably melted to the point at which not much is left other than a few patches of ice.

NASA last week posted images that show glaciers covering 4.31 km2 atop Puncak Jaya in 1988, and another from this year that shows most of that ice is gone. Images from September 2025 apparently showed just .09km2 of ice remained. 

“To qualify as a glacier, a body of ice generally has to be thick enough to flow downhill under its own weight, and it needs an area where snow builds up faster than it melts,” NASA’s Kathryn Hansen wrote. “Puncak Jaya’s remaining ice has thinned so much and broken into such small, stagnant patches that it no longer flows.”

For what it’s worth, commercial operators run expeditions to Puncak Jaya. Peak-baggers seek it out because some consider it the highest mountain in Australasia/Oceania and therefore one of the “Seven Summits” –  the highest point on each continent.

The Reg won’t get into the debate about the validity of including Puncak Jaya on that list, but if you fancy some equatorial alpine action your correspondent recently climbed Malaysia’s 4,095m Mount Kinabalu. It’s an overnight walk that requires no technical skills or gear, but definitely demands supple knees. The peak was clearly glaciated in the distant past but snow is now extremely rare on Kinabalu.

Australian bank giving away its bug-hunter

Here’s an odd one: Australia’s Commonwealth Bank (CBA) created an AI-powered tool to scan its bespoke code for bugs, and has now packaged it as a free release called “CodeCheck.”

The bank says analyzes the output of OpenAI’s Codex and Anthropic’s Claude Code with “a consistent process for analyzing code, investigating potential vulnerabilities and providing information to assist engineers.” Apparently, it is “ based on an approach used within CBA, but it is not the same as, and does not represent, the systems, tools or controls CBA uses internally.”

The bank posted CodeCheck to GitHub, where it warns the project is “a one-time open-source release for businesses to evaluate” and that it will not actively maintain, update, or support the code.

Japan’s space program hands some launches to Mitsubishi

Japan’s Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) last week announced it has reached an agreement with Mitsubishi Heavy Industries (MHI) to take over responsibility for running launches of its flagship H3 rocket when used in certain configurations.

The deal means MHI will handle launches for H3s that use a pair of LE-9 liquid-fuel engines alongside two SRB-3 solid-fuel boosters.

JAXA will continue running launches that use different, or experimental, configurations.

Once JAXA is satisfied those new rigs are reliable, it plans to transition them to private operators, too. ®

item.title: Google claims last week’s critical VMware bug was under attack in September (2026)
item.description:
Google’s Mandiant unit has claimed that the critical flaw VMware last week revealed in its vCenter product was under attack by a China-linked threat actor which knew of the bug in July and exploited it in September.

VMware revealed several flaws on November 19. The big nasty is CVE-2026-123890, which allows unauthorized access to vCenter, the management console for hosts and guest VMs.

According to seven researchers from Google’s threat intelligence group (formerly Mandiant), a crew it calls ARMORY CASTLE that it suspects of having links to the People’s Republic of China exploited CVE-2026-123890 by first compromising remote access appliances from BeyondTrust.

Google’s analysis suggests the crew uses that toehold to establish access to other Linux appliances before moving deeper into victims’ networks.

If the crew finds vCenter, it deploys a custom malware tool called “BONESAW” designed to slice into the VMware product. In the incident Google observed, BONESAW let attackers “forge authentication tokens, bypass MFA, and impersonate any user.”

The gang put that access to work by conducting an inventory of the victim’s VMware setup, scooping up data describing the ESXi file system, attached disks, and mounted Virtual Machine File System volumes. ARMORY CASTLE also added an SSH public key to the root account’s authorized keys, and “conducted further reconnaissance and data theft on the ESXi filesystem using the root account.”

Google also found evidence of BONESAW being used in July, on a server an unidentified entity had patched against CVE-2026-59309 – another authentication bypass vulnerability in vCenter.

And BONESAW was just one of five tools Google thinks ARMORY CASTLE created as part of its plan to attack vCenter. It also made webshells named SLIMSAVAGE and CAGEMATCH, a backdoor called BEARBONES, and a SAML utility called SAWSNAKE.

“The use of three separate specialized sets of malware and two zero-days in the course of a single campaign indicates that there are significant resources supporting ARMORY CASTLE operations,” Google’s researchers wrote. “It also shows the extent of the threat actor’s operational commitment to compromise high priority targets.”

Few targets are as juicy as vCenter, because it can literally give attackers access to thousands of virtual machines and the hosts they run on.

Google hasn't said how many attacks is saw on vCenter using BONESAW. 

The Register asked VMware if it was aware of the September attack, if it took any measures to defend its customers at the time, and to share a timeline for disclosure and remediation of CVE-2026-123890.

A spokesperson responded by pointing to VMware’s Q&A document and stating “In today's threat environment, customers should assume any publicly disclosed critical vulnerability can and will be exploited by threat actors under the right conditions and should apply the recommended patches immediately.”

VMware has tried to make that easier by adding non-disruptive patching to several of its products, and introducing a product called vDefend that offers “virtual patching” by creating compensating controls that use network micro segmentation and other techniques to block access to resources malware uses. Last month, VMware debuted another new tool, HyperArmor, to block incoming malicious traffic targeting its VCF private cloud suite.

In recent discussions with The Register, VMware execs told us the Broadcom business unit will emphasize security improvements in future product releases.

“Our teams have integrated frontier AI security model testing directly into our engineering workflows, strengthened our software supply chain to reduce third-party dependencies and speed up upstream responses, and built VCF 9.1 specifically for high-velocity security,” a spokesperson said in response to questions about the Mandiant report.

Freebie patches hard to find

One security offering VMware won’t continue is free access to patches for zero-day flaws in supported versions of products sold under its old perpetual licenses – even to users who don’t have an ongoing support deal or software subscription.

VMware last year stopped making those patches available for download and promised it would establish “a separate patch delivery cycle.”

Readers have pointed out that information about the new cycle isn’t easy to find, and The Register noticed that the blog post in which Broadcom CEO Hock Tan promised the free patches no longer contains references to the offer. Removing the promise seems to be a recent edit as an Internet Archive snapshot of the page from October 20 does mention the zero-day patch freebies.

A VMware spokesperson told us the free zero-day patch policy remains in place despite changes to the post.

“Broadcom’s policy to provide access to zero-day critical security patches to customers who, at their own risk, continue to run perpetual VMware vSphere 8 software without an active support agreement, remains in place,” the spokesperson wrote. “Those customers can get these patches by contacting Broadcom. This policy covers vSphere 8 patches only and is expected to remain in effect through the end of general support on October 11, 2027.” ®

item.title: When Microsoft, Apple, and the FAA can't keep it up, it's a system of a down (2026)
item.description:
No Access November is going well this year.

Among the many organizations to adopt Outage As A Service (OAAS) were Microsoft, Apple, the FAA, and any number of European supermarkets. Even the NSA has succumbed. For us, at least, outage is word of the year. It's certainly deeply embedded in the public mind, with schoolchildren reportedly referring to the 19th century Irish famine as "the potato outage." There's no danger of an outrage outage.

OAAS is synonymous with infrastructure failure, a more useful term that begins to hint at cause and cure as well as effect. In all of the latest crop, what we know is depressingly familiar. Microsoft's O365 meltdown was a cascading failure caused by a botched upgrade that took stuff offline and melted down as it tried to come back. The FAA was a migration from Jurassic hardware that wasn't end of life so much as living fossil. The Eurofridge-cum-fondue-maker was a control system so badly written it fell apart if you raised an eyebrow at it. Clearly, nobody had. Until now.

These are all different classes of OAAS that have been around for decades. Security-based outages are still outages, and a packet flood is still a packet flood whether it's a botnet DDoS or finger trouble in the config dashboard.

Each of them has a root cause with obvious fixes – a faulty mental model of network/server interaction, chronic underfunding, a complete supply chain with little cyber-security expertise. All these, like the poor, will be with us always. They won't fix themselves. Infrastructure that works is invisible, and invisible things are forgotten until they break. What's needed is an infrastructure that watches itself, that is designed to be adaptive and resilient, one that refuses to connect to danger and nulls out any that gets through.

There have been attempts to create a ground-up architecture that is inherently risk resistant. One such is SCION (Scalability, Control, and Isolation On Next-generation networks). It redesigns routing between domains around explicit path selection, separate control and data planes, and mechanisms for trust and failure isolation. The result is a very resilient, very reliable, and very secure infrastructure that reflects the designers' tenet that you can't patch the internet into any of these things. Start from scratch or GTFO.

SCION started about 15 years ago, and it works well enough to be adopted by entities like the Secure Swiss Finance Network. If the Gnomes of Zurich trust it, no higher accreditation exists. Well, it was designed by ETH Zürich. Where you won't find it is almost everywhere else. The internet is like Switzerland in the same way the Amazon rainforest is like Central Park. There are trees and sometimes it rains. It is unwise to infer anything else.

Given you can't manicure existing infrastructure into true resilience, the only other option is evolution. A couple of billion years of continued life on Earth has proved this is the only way to re-engineer complex systems while they're usefully running. In this case, the current evolutionary endpoint that's of most interest is the human immune system.

An interlocking system of functions, it takes care of uncountably thousands of pathogen-based threats and internal malfunctions every day. You might think that the 30-odd billion computing machines making up today's Internet are impossible to monitor and secure, but that's peanuts to the human immune system. An average human has around 30 trillion cells, and roughly the same again in bacteria. When it works, the mechanics of the human infrastructure are invisible and out of mind. The immune system makes it so, and everything involved is driven by information, signaling and behavior. There is pattern matching, resource management, defense in depth and reinforcement learning in persistent models. Sounds familiar?

The analogy between this and modern digital infrastructure is so irresistible that it has been around for a lifetime. Viruses, infections, swarms, worms, system health are so familiar that they go unremarked. The term Digital Immune System has been around since the last century too, pushed by outfits like IBM, Symantec and Gartner. It hasn't taken off, probably because it's been marketing bunkum instead of describing the development of inherently resilient infrastructure based on insights from biology.

It has also been true that natural selection, the engine of evolution and this biology, only works in IT at the most macro, capitalist level of product and company survival. Everything else is selected through design decisions, market analysis, and insight versus delusion. The adoption of immunological concepts to digital infrastructure will have to be the result of rigorous exploration of complex systems and cross-disciplinary research. What would that look like?

There are academics thinking just these thoughts: see this paper [PDF] from Kay Smarsly at Technische Universität Hamburg. Like SCION, it takes an architectural look at what resiliency might look like, but with explicit reference to biological systems.

OAAS is a chronic syndrome with multiple causes and potentially fatal outcomes. It exists and persists because digital infrastructure too often fails to contain internal failures or external attacks. We have a working example of an approach to managing analogous problems in systems far vaster and more intricate than any we have built. We now have tools that may start to do systemic analysis and inference at a useful scale. In an industry prepared to bet billions on agents that do your shopping, there is every reason to kick off serious research into digital immune systems worthy of the name. Doctor, cure thyself. ®

The FAA was a migration from Jurassic hardware that wasn't end of life so much as living fossil. The Eurofridge-cum-fondue-maker was a control system so badly written it fell apart if you raised an eyebrow at it. Clearly, nobody had. Until now.

These are all different classes of OAAS that have been around for decades. Security-based outages are still outages, and a packet flood is still a packet flood whether it's a botnet DDoS or finger trouble in the config dashboard.

Each of them has a root cause with obvious fixes – a faulty mental model of network/server interaction, chronic underfunding, a complete supply chain with little cyber-security expertise. All these, like the poor, will be with us always. They won't fix themselves. Infrastructure that works is invisible, and invisible things are forgotten until they break. What's needed is an infrastructure that watches itself, that is designed to be adaptive and resilient, one that refuses to connect to danger and nulls out any that gets through.

There have been attempts to create a ground-up architecture that is inherently risk resistant. One such is SCION (Scalability, Control, and Isolation On Next-generation networks). It redesigns routing between domains around explicit path selection, separate control and data planes, and mechanisms for trust and failure isolation. The result is a very resilient, very reliable, and very secure infrastructure that reflects the designers' tenet that you can't patch the internet into any of these things. Start from scratch or GTFO.

SCION started about 15 years ago, and it works well enough to be adopted by entities like the Secure Swiss Finance Network. If the Gnomes of Zurich trust it, no higher accreditation exists. Well, it was designed by ETH Zürich. Where you won't find it is almost everywhere else. The internet is like Switzerland in the same way the Amazon rainforest is like Central Park. There are trees and sometimes it rains. It is unwise to infer anything else.

Given you can't manicure existing infrastructure into true resilience, the only other option is evolution. A couple of billion years of continued life on Earth has proved this is the only way to re-engineer complex systems while they're usefully running. In this case, the current evolutionary endpoint that's of most interest is the human immune system.

An interlocking system of functions, it takes care of uncountably thousands of pathogen-based threats and internal malfunctions every day. You might think that the 30-odd billion computing machines making up today's Internet are impossible to monitor and secure, but that's peanuts to the human immune system. An average human has around 30 trillion cells, and roughly the same again in bacteria. When it works, the mechanics of the human infrastructure are invisible and out of mind. The immune system makes it so, and everything involved is driven by information, signaling and behavior. There is pattern matching, resource management, defense in depth and reinforcement learning in persistent models. Sounds familiar?

The analogy between this and modern digital infrastructure is so irresistible that it has been around for a lifetime. Viruses, infections, swarms, worms, system health are so familiar that they go unremarked. The term Digital Immune System has been around since the last century too, pushed by outfits like IBM, Symantec and Gartner. It hasn't taken off, probably because it's been marketing bunkum instead of describing the development of inherently resilient infrastructure based on insights from biology.

It has also been true that natural selection, the engine of evolution and this biology, only works in IT at the most macro, capitalist level of product and company survival. Everything else is selected through design decisions, market analysis, and insight versus delusion. The adoption of immunological concepts to digital infrastructure will have to be the result of rigorous exploration of complex systems and cross-disciplinary research. What would that look like?

There are academics thinking just these thoughts: see this paper [PDF] from Kay Smarsly at Technische Universität Hamburg. Like SCION, it takes an architectural look at what resiliency might look like, but with explicit reference to biological systems.

OAAS is a chronic syndrome with multiple causes and potentially fatal outcomes. It exists and persists because digital infrastructure too often fails to contain internal failures or external attacks. We have a working example of an approach to managing analogous problems in systems far vaster and more intricate than any we have built. We now have tools that may start to do systemic analysis and inference at a useful scale. In an industry prepared to bet billions on agents that do your shopping, there is every reason to kick off serious research into digital immune systems worthy of the name. Doctor, cure thyself. ®

item.title: Cleverbridge admits attackers stole customers' credit card and CVV numbers. Yep, you read that right (2026)
item.description:
Software e-commerce platform Cleverbridge has admitted that hackers stole customers' card numbers and CVV security codes, raising questions about how the attackers captured data that payment security rules prohibit retaining after authorization.

The Germany-headquartered company, which handles software sales and subscriptions on behalf of other businesses, detected unauthorized activity on its platform on November 4. In an incident update, Cleverbridge said it had cut off the intruders' access and launched an investigation that later established payment card information had been copied from its systems.

The public notice doesn't spell out exactly what was stolen, but an email sent to affected customers, seen by The Register, fills in some rather important blanks.

"Based on our investigation to date, the information involved includes payment card details you used to make a purchase through Cleverbridge, notably your card number, expiry date, card security code (CVV/CVC), and contact details," the company told customers.

Email addresses, billing addresses, and phone numbers were also among the information potentially exposed, although Cleverbridge reckons account passwords escaped the breach.

More concerning are the stolen CVV codes. PCI DSS rules prohibit retaining card verification codes after authorization, even in encrypted form.

Cleverbridge hasn't explained how the attackers obtained the codes, whether they were retained after transactions, or whether the criminals intercepted them during payment processing. The company didn't respond to The Register's questions about the breach.

Cleverbridge handles the business of selling software online, from taking payments to managing subscriptions, and its client roster includes some familiar names in enterprise IT, such as Red Hat, SUSE, Tenable, Veeam, Jamf, Parallels, and Plesk. 

That doesn't mean customers of all those companies had their card details stolen. Cleverbridge hasn't named the vendors affected by the intrusion, nor has it disclosed how many people were caught up in the breach or how long the hackers were poking around its systems.

In its notification to customers, the company said it had contacted data protection authorities, payment card schemes, and its payment partners, and was working with a specialist police cybercrime unit. It began notifying affected individuals on November 20, more than two weeks after discovering the intrusion.

Affected customers are being offered 24 months of free credit monitoring and fraud assistance. That may help detect identity misuse, but it won't stop a crook armed with their card number, expiration date, and CVV from attempting a fraudulent purchase.

Two years of credit monitoring is a nice gesture, but customers whose card numbers and CVVs are now in criminal hands might prefer a new bit of plastic. ®
